escenas.titulo: Productivity: new biomass per unit time

visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: gross or net, primary or secondary, and their formulas

turnos.t: Part two: productivity.
According to Codony, productivity is the conversion of energy in an ecosystem into biomass over a given period of time.
The key word is time: productivity is a rate.
That's why its units always include time: kilojoules per square metre per year if you measure it as energy, or grams per square metre per year if you measure it as dry biomass.
Biomass on its own, by contrast, is a stock: what's there at one moment.
Productivity can be gross, what is produced before any losses, or net, what's left after the losses.
And each of those can be primary, from the plants, or secondary, from the animals.

visual.titulo: Gross and net productivity: worked example
visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: temperate grassland, NPP = 2000 − 800 = 1200 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹

turnos.t: Gross primary productivity is the total gain in energy or biomass, per unit area per unit time, made by producers through photosynthesis.
But plants respire and use some of it up.
Net primary productivity is what's left after subtracting those respiratory losses.
The formula: net primary productivity equals gross primary productivity minus respiration.
Here's the example from class: a temperate grassland.
Gross primary productivity: two thousand grams of carbon per square metre per year.
Respiration: eight hundred.
Net primary productivity: two thousand minus eight hundred, which is one thousand two hundred.
So each square metre adds one point two kilograms of plant biomass a year for the herbivores.
That's why net is always smaller than gross.

visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: food 200, faeces 100, GSP 100, respiration 67, NSP 33

turnos.t: Now the consumers, with one extra step: they don't absorb everything they eat.
Gross secondary productivity is what the consumer absorbs: food eaten minus faeces.
And net secondary productivity is what it actually stores as new biomass: gross secondary productivity minus respiration.
Two formulas, in that order.
The example on the slide: the consumer eats two hundred units and loses a hundred in its faeces, so its gross secondary productivity is a hundred.
It respires sixty-seven, so the net secondary productivity is a hundred minus sixty-seven: thirty-three.
The typical mistake is forgetting the faeces.
Faeces first, then respiration.

escenas.titulo: Calculate with me: two exam questions

turnos.t: Two exam-style questions.
First: a population of rabbits eats two hundred and fifty kilojoules of grass, loses ninety in faeces and a hundred and twenty in respiration.
Calculate the net secondary productivity.
Step one: gross secondary productivity, two hundred and fifty minus ninety, a hundred and sixty kilojoules.
Step two: net, a hundred and sixty minus a hundred and twenty, forty kilojoules.
If you just write forty, you get one mark out of two.
Name each step and include units.
Second: a meadow has a gross primary productivity of two thousand five hundred kilojoules per square metre per year, and respires one thousand five hundred.
What percentage becomes net?
The net is one thousand.
One thousand divided by two thousand five hundred, times a hundred: forty per cent.

visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: one oak feeds many insects, so the base is narrow

turnos.t: On to ecological pyramids.
A food web is qualitative: it tells you who eats whom.
A pyramid is quantitative: it measures something at each trophic level.
There are three: numbers, biomass and energy.
The pyramid of numbers shows abundance, the number of individuals at each level of a food chain, regardless of their size.
And that's exactly why it can be inverted.
A single oak tree feeds a huge number of insects, so the base is very narrow.
The Kognity example: one oak, two hundred and fifty caterpillars, twenty birds and two hawks.
Codony gives two cases of inverted pyramids: beetles feeding on forest trees, and parasites living on large host animals.

visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: both measure amounts at one moment and can be inverted

turnos.t: The pyramid of biomass shows the biomass present at each trophic level of a community at a particular moment, in grams per square metre.
It's a snapshot, a stock: the standing crop.
It's usually upright, but it can be inverted.
Codony's example is a pond.
At any given moment, the mass of phytoplankton, the producers, is smaller than the mass of the heterotrophs that eat it, like fish and insects.
The same happens in the sea with zooplankton.
How is that possible?
Because phytoplankton reproduce very quickly, but each individual lives for a very short time.
They're replaced so fast that a small biomass at any instant produces a lot of energy over time.

visual.titulo: Pyramids of energy are always upright
visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: oak 1,000 → caterpillar 100 → sparrow 10 → sparrowhawk 1 (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹)

turnos.t: The third is the pyramid of energy, which some books call the pyramid of productivity.
It shows the flow of energy through each trophic level, per unit area per unit time: kilojoules per square metre per year.
It doesn't measure what's there, but what passes through.
It's a rate, not a stock.
And because energy is lost as heat at every transfer, by the second law, each level always receives less than the one below.
That's why a pyramid of energy is never, ever inverted.
The example from class: oak, a thousand kilojoules; caterpillar, a hundred; sparrow, ten; sparrowhawk, one.

escenas.titulo: Stock or rate: why some pyramids invert

visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: at sea, numbers and biomass invert at the base; energy does not

turnos.t: A classic seven-mark question.
With grass, rabbit and fox, all three pyramids are upright.
In the sea, with phytoplankton at the base, the pyramids of numbers and biomass get narrow at the bottom; the energy pyramid doesn't.
The key is stock versus rate.
Numbers and biomass are snapshots, so a huge producer, or one that's replaced very quickly, distorts them.
Energy is a flow over time, and it obeys the second law.
That's why Codony says the pyramid of energy is the most useful.
It takes the rate of production into account.
It lets you compare species with similar biomass but very different lifespans.
It lets you compare ecosystems.
It's never inverted.
And you can add solar energy input at the base.

visual.titulo: Human impacts on flows: persistent pollutants
visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: DDT, PCBs and heavy metals in food webs

turnos.t: Final part: how humans alter these flows.
First, persistent, non-biodegradable pollutants: pesticides like D D T, or heavy metals like mercury.
Bioaccumulation: the pollutant builds up inside a single organism over time, because it's absorbed faster than it's removed.
One organism, over time.
Biomagnification: the concentration increases at each higher trophic level. Why?
Because each predator eats many contaminated prey and keeps the pollutant from all of them.
The case study from class is Minamata Bay, in Japan.
Between nineteen thirty-two and nineteen sixty-eight, a factory released methylmercury, which passed through fish and shellfish all the way to people.

visual.pie: Microplastics found inside a fish (Codony, T2C2)

turnos.t: Another pollutant: microplastics, plastic particles smaller than five millimetres.
They come from plastic waste reaching the sea, where water, salt and sunlight break it into tiny pieces; from washing synthetic fabrics; and from industrial discharges.
Filter feeders, the animals that filter water for food, take them in, and other animals eat them by mistake.
Larger particles block the digestive tract.
Smaller ones are assimilated, then bioaccumulate and biomagnify.
On top of that, they can carry other pollutants and additives stuck to them, so they increase the chance that those pollutants travel through the food web.

visual.titulo: Human activities alter energy and matter flows
visual.pie: Codony, T2C2: four pressures that change production, cycles and food webs

turnos.t: Four human pressures change these flows.
Fossil fuels: more carbon dioxide, warming, and altered abiotic conditions.
Deforestation: we lose producers, carbon stores and evapotranspiration.
Urbanisation: it replaces habitats and fragments food webs.
And agriculture: it simplifies food webs, and when we harvest, we export biomass and nutrients.
All of this changes the resilience of the ecosystem.
Climate change has two sides.
Higher temperatures and more carbon dioxide can speed up photosynthesis and widen the base of the pyramid, which can unbalance aquatic ecosystems.
But drought, extreme heat and other pollutants can reduce productivity.
And habitat loss removes plant biomass, shelter and camouflage.

turnos.t: For the exam, here are the typical questions.
Explain how the second law limits food chains, four marks: the law itself, the losses as heat and in faeces, the ten per cent that varies, and that after four or five levels there's no energy left.
Calculate net secondary productivity: two named steps, with units.
Why is net primary productivity smaller than gross?
Because producers respire, and that energy is lost as heat.
The seven-marker on pyramids: what each one measures and in what units, the second law, stock versus rate, and the oak and phytoplankton examples.
D D T in top predators: persistent, bioaccumulation, many prey, biomagnification.
And climate change: one effect plus its mechanism.
